title: Purple Tree Review: Ingredients, DHM Dose, and Honest Verdict
excerpt: An honest Purple Tree review: what's in the ingredient panel, how its DHM dose compares to standalone DHM, what users say, whether it's worth the money, and who should skip it.
metaDescription: Honest Purple Tree review: what's on the ingredient panel, how its DHM dose compares to standalone DHM, what users say, value, and safety notes.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Purple Tree is a convenient, widely stocked hangover supplement built around DHM (dihydromyricetin), the plant compound with the most interesting research behind it in this category. Its main weakness is the same one most multi-ingredient "party" supplements share: the label doesn't make it easy to tell exactly how much DHM you get per serving, and what research exists on DHM used doses that may be higher than what a small combo capsule delivers. If you value grab-and-go packs and like the idea of a blended formula, it's a reasonable buy. If you want the most DHM for your money and a dose you can verify, a standalone DHM capsule is usually the better deal.

**Who it suits:** occasional drinkers who want something small to carry to a wedding, a bar, or a flight. **Who should skip it:** people who want a clearly labeled, research-matched DHM dose, people on a tight budget, and anyone who takes regular medication without first checking with a pharmacist.

> **Not medical advice.** Hangover supplements are sold as dietary supplements, which means the FDA does not review them for safety or effectiveness before they go on sale. No supplement makes heavy drinking safe or lowers your blood alcohol level. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before trying Purple Tree or any DHM product if** you are pregnant or breastfeeding, have liver or kidney disease, take prescription medication (especially sedatives, blood thinners, antidepressants, or seizure medicines), or drink heavily on a regular basis. If you or someone else shows signs of alcohol poisoning (confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, cold or bluish skin, or can't be woken), call 911.

We don't sell or link to Purple Tree, and we earn nothing from it. This review is based on how the product is marketed and labeled, on what the published research says about its key ingredients, and on the general themes in public customer feedback.

## What Purple Tree Is

Purple Tree markets itself as a "celebration vitamin": a supplement you take around drinking to help you feel better the next day. You'll typically find it in small single-serving packs as well as larger bottles, and it's sold in places hangover products don't usually reach, such as convenience stores, airport shops, and some liquor stores, as well as online.

That retail reach is a real part of the appeal. A lot of people first meet Purple Tree at a checkout counter, not after researching DHM. It's a brand that lives in the same shelf space as energy shots and electrolyte drinks.

Like every product in this category, Purple Tree is a dietary supplement, not a drug. In the US, supplement makers are not allowed to claim their products prevent or cure a hangover as a disease, which is why the packaging tends to use softer words like "support," "recovery," and "feel better tomorrow." That's not a knock on Purple Tree specifically. It's how the whole category is regulated, and it's worth knowing when you read any hangover product's marketing.

## The Ingredient Panel: What's Inside

Purple Tree's formula is built around **DHM**, sourced from the Japanese raisin tree (*Hovenia dulcis*), combined with supporting ingredients that have commonly included B vitamins and other compounds marketed for alcohol metabolism or antioxidant support. Formulas in this category change over time, and the version on the shelf near you may not match an older listing online, so treat the box in your hand as the final word.

Here's how to read the label, and what each type of ingredient can and can't do.

### DHM (dihydromyricetin)

This is the ingredient doing most of the heavy lifting in the marketing, and the one with the most research behind it.

**What the research shows:** The most-cited study is a 2012 paper in the *Journal of Neuroscience* by Shen and colleagues at UCLA. In rats, DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal, and the authors linked this to DHM's effects on GABA-A receptors, the same brain receptors alcohol acts on. Later lab and animal work has looked at DHM's effects on alcohol-processing enzymes in the liver and on markers of liver stress. The human record is much smaller. A 2015 randomized trial in people with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease found improvements in some liver markers, but that study was about fatty liver, not hangovers.

**What it doesn't show:** There is no large, well-controlled human trial showing that DHM prevents hangovers. Much of what you read online, including on some brand websites, takes rat results and presents them as if they were proven in people. They aren't yet. The honest summary is that DHM is promising, plausible, and generally well tolerated in the studies that exist, but not proven.

For a deeper look at the research and dosing, see our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025).

### B vitamins

Many hangover formulas include B vitamins such as thiamine (B1), riboflavin (B2), niacin (B3), and B6. The reasoning is that heavy drinking can deplete some B vitamins, and several are involved in energy metabolism.

That's true as far as it goes, but there's little evidence that taking B vitamins on the night of drinking changes how you feel the next morning. A small study from the early 1970s tested a vitamin B6 derivative (pyritinol) and reported fewer hangover symptoms, but it was tiny, old, and hasn't been convincingly repeated. B vitamins are cheap, safe at normal doses, and unlikely to hurt. Just don't count them as the reason a product works.

### Amino acids and antioxidants

Combination hangover products often add ingredients like L-cysteine or N-acetylcysteine (NAC), milk thistle, prickly pear, or ginger. The appeal is easy to see: alcohol breaks down into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product, and some of these compounds have been studied for their role in clearing it or for reducing inflammation.

The research is mixed and mostly small. Prickly pear (*Opuntia ficus indica*) is the best-known example: a 2004 study in *Archives of Internal Medicine* found it reduced some hangover symptoms, mainly nausea and dry mouth, but not headache or overall misery. We compare the two directly in our [DHM vs prickly pear guide](/never-hungover/dhm-vs-prickly-pear-hangovers).

Whatever supporting ingredients your box lists, the key question is the same: are they present in amounts that match the studies, or are they there to make the label look full? With small capsules and long ingredient lists, it's often the latter.

### The proprietary blend problem

This is the biggest thing to check on any multi-ingredient hangover product, including Purple Tree. Many supplements group several ingredients under a single "proprietary blend" line with one total weight. The rules require the blend's total to be listed and the ingredients to be in descending order by weight, but not the amount of each one.

If DHM sits inside a blend, you can't know whether you're getting a meaningful dose or a token amount. A 500 mg blend with six ingredients could contain 300 mg of DHM or 50 mg. The label simply doesn't tell you.

So when you pick up a box, look for this:

- **Is DHM listed with its own milligram amount?** If yes, good. You can compare it against other products.
- **Is it inside a blend?** Then the most you can say is that DHM is somewhere below the blend's total weight.
- **How many capsules is one serving?** A serving of two or three capsules changes the per-pill math.
- **Is the DHM content standardized?** "Hovenia dulcis extract" is not always the same thing as pure DHM. An extract can contain anywhere from a small share to a large share of actual DHM, depending on how it's made. Some labels state a percentage; many don't.

## Dose Reality: Purple Tree vs Standalone DHM

Here's the crux of this review. The single most important number for a DHM product is how much actual DHM you get, and how that compares to what people typically use.

There's no official recommended dose of DHM. The human studies that exist have used a range of amounts, and most standalone DHM products on the market sell 300 mg to 1,000 mg per serving. Our dosage guide suggests that many people use roughly 300 mg to 600 mg before drinking, with some taking a second dose before bed. That's a practical starting point based on what's sold and what's been studied, not a medically established dose.

Combination products like Purple Tree tend to land at the lower end of that range or don't disclose a single figure, because they're trying to fit several ingredients into one small serving. That's the trade-off you're making.

| | Combination product (like Purple Tree) | Standalone DHM capsule |
|---|---|---|
| DHM per serving | Often lower, or not stated separately | Usually 300 to 1,000 mg, clearly listed |
| Other ingredients | Several, often in small amounts | Usually none, or one or two |
| Can you verify the DHM dose? | Sometimes not, if it's in a blend | Yes |
| Convenience | High: single-serve packs, sold in stores | Lower: mostly online, in bottles |
| Cost per mg of DHM | Generally higher | Generally lower |
| Easy to adjust your dose? | Harder, because you get more of everything | Easy: take one or two capsules |

None of this means Purple Tree doesn't work. It means you're paying partly for convenience and for a blend of extras with weak evidence, rather than purely for DHM.

If DHM is the reason you're buying, a standalone capsule gives you more of it for less. Two widely available options are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a plain, budget-friendly 1,000 mg product, and [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which pairs DHM with a few supporting ingredients but lists its DHM amount. We compare those two head to head in our [Double Wood vs No Days Wasted comparison](/never-hungover/double-wood-vs-no-days-wasted-dhm-comparison-2025).

## What Users Say: A Fair Summary of Sentiment

We don't have access to a verified, representative survey of Purple Tree users, and star ratings on retail sites are easy to game in this category. So instead of quoting a number, here are the themes that show up again and again in public feedback about Purple Tree and similar combination hangover supplements.

**What people like:**

- **Convenience.** The single-serve packs are the most praised feature. People like having one in a wallet or bag without carrying a bottle.
- **Availability.** Being able to buy it at a store on the way to an event matters to a lot of buyers.
- **"I felt better than expected."** Plenty of reviewers say they woke up feeling less rough than usual after a night out.

**What people complain about:**

- **Inconsistent results.** A common pattern is "worked great the first time, did nothing the second." That's typical of hangover products in general, because how you feel the next day depends heavily on how much you drank, what you ate, how much you slept, and how hydrated you were.
- **Price.** Per serving, combination packs often cost noticeably more than standalone DHM capsules.
- **It doesn't work after heavy drinking.** Reviewers who drank a lot often report that no supplement saved them. That matches what the science would predict.

### How to read those reviews

Hangover reviews are especially hard to trust, for reasons that have nothing to do with any one brand:

1. **No comparison night.** People rarely drink the exact same amount on a night without the supplement, so they can't tell what the product did.
2. **The placebo effect is strong for hangovers.** Taking anything, plus the extra glass of water that often comes with it, can make people feel more in control and more careful.
3. **Behavior changes.** Someone who remembered to take a supplement is often the same person who also drank water and ate dinner.

That doesn't mean the positive reviews are wrong. It means they can't separate the product from everything else that happened that night.

## Value: Is Purple Tree Worth the Money?

Prices change often and vary by store, so we won't quote a specific figure that could be out of date by the time you read this. The useful way to judge value is to do the math yourself:

1. **Find the price per serving.** Divide the box price by the number of servings (not capsules).
2. **Find the DHM per serving.** If the label lists it separately, use that number. If DHM is inside a blend, you can't do this step, and that's a point against it.
3. **Compare cost per 100 mg of DHM** against a standalone product.

When we run this exercise on combination hangover products in general, the standalone DHM capsules nearly always come out cheaper per milligram, often by a wide margin. Where combination packs win is convenience: if you would otherwise forget to take anything, a pack you actually use is worth more than a bottle sitting at home.

**Our view:** Purple Tree is fair value as an occasional convenience purchase, and poor value as your regular DHM source.

## Pros and Cons

**Pros**

- Built around DHM, the hangover-supplement ingredient with the most interesting research
- Single-serve packs are genuinely convenient for nights out and travel
- Widely sold in physical stores, so you can buy it on the day
- Supporting ingredients like B vitamins are low risk at normal doses
- Generally well tolerated, based on the safety profile of its main ingredients

**Cons**

- DHM amount may be hard to verify if it sits inside a proprietary blend
- Likely less DHM per dollar than a standalone capsule
- Supporting ingredients have weak or mixed evidence for hangovers
- Results vary a lot from night to night, as with every hangover product
- Like all supplements, not reviewed by the FDA for effectiveness before sale

## Safety: Who Should Be Careful

DHM has been well tolerated in the small human studies that exist, and serious side effects haven't been a common theme. But "well tolerated in small studies" is not the same as "safe for everyone," and a combination product adds more variables.

Be careful, and check with a doctor or pharmacist first, if you:

- **Take prescription medication.** DHM acts on GABA receptors in animal studies and may affect how the liver processes some drugs. That's a reason to ask before combining it with sedatives, sleep medicines, anti-anxiety drugs, antidepressants, or seizure medicines. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers this in more detail.
- **Take blood thinners.** Some ingredients common in hangover blends, such as willow bark or ginkgo if present, can affect bleeding. Read the full label.
- **Have liver or kidney disease.** Ask your doctor before adding any supplement.
- **Are pregnant or breastfeeding.** There's no good safety data for DHM in pregnancy.

**Two important reminders:**

- **Purple Tree does not lower your blood alcohol level** and does not make it safe to drive. Nothing in a capsule speeds up how fast your body clears alcohol enough to matter for safety.
- **Don't combine hangover supplements with painkillers "just in case."** In particular, avoid taking acetaminophen while drinking. Our guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains why.

## How to Use It (If You Try It)

If you decide to try Purple Tree, a sensible approach looks like this:

- **Follow the label directions.** Most DHM products suggest taking them during or after drinking. Don't exceed the serving size.
- **Pair it with the basics.** Eat a proper meal before drinking, alternate alcoholic drinks with water, and stop at a reasonable point. These habits have stronger evidence than any supplement. Our [how to prevent a hangover guide](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what actually helps.
- **Test it fairly.** If you want to know whether it does anything for you, try it on two similar nights, one with and one without, keeping drinks, food, and sleep as similar as you can.
- **Judge it on moderate nights.** No supplement rescues a very heavy night. If a product only "fails" when you drank twice your usual amount, that's not really a fair test.

## How Purple Tree Compares to Other Brands

Purple Tree sits in a crowded field. Here's a quick, plain-language map of where it falls.

- **Versus standalone DHM (Double Wood, NusaPure, Toniiq Ease and similar):** Standalone capsules give you more verifiable DHM for less money. Purple Tree wins on convenience and store availability.
- **Versus Flyby:** Flyby is another multi-ingredient formula built around DHM, sold mostly online. Our [Flyby review](/never-hungover/flyby-recovery-review-2025) goes through its label in detail; the same questions about dose and blends apply to both.
- **Versus No Days Wasted:** No Days Wasted also blends DHM with supporting ingredients but lists its DHM amount clearly. See our [No Days Wasted review](/never-hungover/no-days-wasted-dhm-review-analysis).
- **Versus Cheers Restore:** Cheers is another well-known DHM-based brand that uses its own formulation. We cover it in our [Cheers Restore review](/never-hungover/cheers-restore-review).
- **Versus ZBiotics:** ZBiotics takes a different approach entirely, using an engineered probiotic aimed at acetaldehyde rather than DHM. See our [ZBiotics review](/never-hungover/zbiotics-review).
- **Versus hangover patches:** Patches are a separate category with weaker evidence still. We look at them in [do hangover patches work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work).

For the full picture of which ingredients have real evidence behind them, see our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025).

## The Verdict

Purple Tree is a legitimate, convenient product built around the right headline ingredient. It isn't a scam, and many people like it. But it's sold on convenience more than on dose, and the research on hangover supplements, DHM included, is still early.

- **Buy it if** you want a small, ready-to-go pack for occasional nights out and you value being able to pick it up in a store.
- **Skip it if** you want a clearly labeled, higher DHM dose, or if you take supplements regularly and care about cost per serving. A standalone DHM capsule will serve you better.
- **Either way,** check the current label for how much DHM is actually listed, talk to a pharmacist if you take medication, and remember that the most reliable hangover prevention is still drinking less, eating first, and drinking water alongside.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does Purple Tree actually work for hangovers?**

It may help some people, but there's no strong clinical evidence that Purple Tree, or any hangover supplement, reliably prevents hangovers. Its main ingredient, DHM, has promising animal research and limited human data. Many users report feeling better, but those reports can't separate the product from other factors like food, water, sleep, and how much was drunk.

**How much DHM is in Purple Tree?**

Check the current label on your box. If DHM is listed with its own milligram amount, you can compare it directly with other products. If it sits inside a proprietary blend, the label only tells you the total weight of the blend, so you can't know the exact DHM dose. Formulas can change over time, so older online listings may not match what's on the shelf.

**Is Purple Tree better than a standalone DHM supplement?**

For convenience, often yes: single-serve packs and store availability are its strengths. For dose and value, usually no. Standalone DHM capsules typically provide more DHM per serving, list the amount clearly, and cost less per milligram. If DHM is the reason you're buying, a standalone capsule is generally the better deal.

**When should I take Purple Tree?**

Follow the directions on the label. Most DHM products are meant to be taken during or after drinking. Don't take more than the listed serving size, and don't combine it with painkillers like acetaminophen while you're drinking.

**Is Purple Tree safe?**

Its main ingredients have been generally well tolerated in the limited studies available, but supplements aren't reviewed by the FDA for safety or effectiveness before sale. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medication, have liver or kidney disease, take blood thinners, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. Purple Tree does not lower blood alcohol or make it safe to drive.

**Why do some people say Purple Tree stopped working?**

Hangover severity depends heavily on how much you drank, what you ate, how well you slept, and how hydrated you were, so results vary from night to night with any product. A supplement that seemed to work after a moderate night will often seem to fail after a heavy one. Testing it on two similar nights, one with and one without, is the fairest way to judge it.

**Where can I buy Purple Tree?**

Purple Tree is sold in many physical stores, including convenience stores, airport shops, and some liquor stores, as well as online. We don't sell it or link to it. If you're mainly after DHM, our [hangover supplements guide](/never-hungover/hangover-supplements-complete-guide-what-actually-works-2025) compares standalone options.
